abstract: This study examines how different content features in political campaign posts influenced user engagement across Facebook, Instagram, and Twitter during Norway's 2021 parliamentary election. Using a manual content analysis of 2,197 posts from nine parties and their leaders, the authors assess how three content types — calls to action, policy topics, and populist styles — affected the number of likes, treated as a cross-platform functional equivalent of low-threshold engagement. The results reveal platform-specific dynamics: calls to action worked best on Twitter, populist exclusion of out-groups worked best on Facebook, and policy topics generally had limited or negative effects across all platforms.
key_claims: User engagement with political campaign content is platform-specific: the same content type triggers different responses on Facebook, Instagram, and Twitter.
Calls to action (informing and mobilizing) generated more likes on Twitter but not on Facebook or Instagram.
Populist styles — specifically the exclusion of out-groups — were most effective at generating engagement on Facebook, the platform argued to privilege populism.
Policy topics generally fail to engage users; when significant, they more often decrease than increase likes across all platforms.
Posts by party leaders received more likes than posts by the parties themselves, consistent across all three platforms.
Observed platform differences, while real, are less distinct than prior literature would suggest.
methods: Standardized manual content analysis of 2,197 posts (Facebook: 1,106; Instagram: 576; Twitter: 515) from nine Norwegian parliamentary parties and their leaders during the 2021 election.
Data collected via the CrowdTangle API (Facebook, Instagram) and the Twitter academic research API; deleted posts and retweets removed.

Content coded for three concepts: calls to action (informing, mobilizing, interacting), 37 topics (reduced to 22 issue categories), and populist styles (people-centrism, anti-elitism, exclusion of out-groups) based on Reinemann et al.'s framework.
Indices created for calls-to-action and populist dimensions by summing coded categories and dividing by total possible variables (range 0 to 1).
Number of likes used as the dependent variable, treated as a functionally equivalent cross-platform engagement metric.
Three separate negative binomial regressions (one per platform) with controls for party vs. party leader, populist (Progress Party) status, and 2021 vote percentage.
Intercoder reliability assessed on 140 posts (5.4%) using Brennan and Prediger's kappa, with reliability between .781 and 1.
findings: On Facebook, the informing index negatively affected likes, while the exclusion-of-out-groups index was significant and positive; the populist Progress Party, party leaders, and larger parties all gained significantly more likes.

On Instagram, the interacting index negatively affected likes, the Progress Party had no advantage, and more topics had negative than positive effects (e.g., rural, education, environmental, defense, and immigration policy negative; economic inequality and foreign policy positive).
On Twitter, both informing and mobilizing indices positively predicted likes; no populist style was significant (the Progress Party was absent from Twitter), and party size was not significant.
H1a and H1b (informing and mobilizing positive on Twitter) supported; H1c (interacting) not supported.
Only H2c (exclusion of out-groups positive on Facebook) among the populism hypotheses was supported.
Across all platforms, very few policy topics engaged users, and significant topic effects were more often negative than positive.
So-called wedge issues (immigration/integration and environmental policy) showed significant negative effects only on Instagram.
contributions: Provides a rare cross-platform comparative analysis of how multiple content types jointly affect user engagement, moving beyond single-content-type studies.
Uses likes as a functionally equivalent engagement metric to enable systematic comparison across Facebook, Instagram, and Twitter.
Offers empirical evidence from a non-US, multiparty European (Norwegian) context, contrasting with the US-dominated literature.
Documents 2021 Twitter engagement patterns that now have historical value given the platform's transformation into X and its decline in Norwegian campaigning.

Suggests practical implications for campaign strategists (vary populist style and calls to action by platform; policy content rarely boosts engagement) and directions for future research on topic clustering, issue ownership, and newer platforms.
framing: The paper positions itself within political communication and social media campaigning research, drawing on the concepts of platform affordances/opportunity structures, populist communication styles (Reinemann et al.; de Vreese et al.), and calls to action. It explicitly answers calls for comparative cross-platform approaches and uses Norway as a case to test the hybrid media landscape beyond the exceptional US context.
